title: Association of fentanyl test strip results and change in drug use behaviors: A multi-state, community-based observational study

claims.statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines; most of the sources also involved opioids or stimulants), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. About half of the drug-checking sources (5 or 6 of 11 by the review's table, editors' count) tested how well drug-checking methods, mostly portable or point-of-care instruments checked against laboratory analysis, detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group (Park et al., 2020, read in full), among 68 of 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids in Baltimore, followed up on average 56 days (not one month, as the review says) after receiving fentanyl test strips with training, counselling and naloxone, reported using alone fell from 95 to 68 in 100 (among the 59 who used opioids at follow-up; the review's 96% is the figure for all 103 at the start) and benzodiazepine use from 22 to 7 in 100; but the baseline drug-use questions covered six months and the follow-up questions one month, the counselling and insert card themselves addressed using alone and mixing other drugs with opioids, the women who used no strip also reduced daily opioid use (9 of 11 to 4 of 11), and overdose, the study's main planned outcome, did not change significantly (6 to 1 women). In an observational study of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in three US states, followed for 28 days in 2023 (Gelberg et al., 2025, read in full), a fentanyl test-strip result showing fentanyl, compared with one not showing it, went with more reports of using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, and the contrast in the amount people reported using was largest when the drugs tested included illicit benzodiazepines (odds ratio 19.9 for reporting less rather than the same or more, against 2.2 for opioids alone); after a result not showing fentanyl on such drugs, using more was reported in a modelled 66 in 100 cases (37 in 100 for opioids alone). The fold reductions that the paper's abstract, and the review's table, give are these odds ratios, not measured falls in the amount used; the study relates self-reported results to self-reported behaviour, measures neither harm nor overdose and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses (an evaluation the review cites as a preprint), and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer than those prescribed none or only briefly (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment than those prescribed none (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; the review's table says the occasionally prescribed group had the lowest in-treatment death rate, without a figure), but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use, along with falls in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people with long-term use of several drugs, in a qualitative study, described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors call drug checking the most widely reported approach, with consistently positive outcomes, and the results of prescribing and policy approaches mixed, without having appraised any source; they find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment, and note that their search, built on the term harm reduction, may have missed studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: of 555 samples, 15 were expected to be benzodiazepines, and benzodiazepine-type drugs were found in 116; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up on average 56 days later; Park et al., read in full): using alone 94.9% to 67.8% (n = 59), benzodiazepine use 22.1% to 7.4%, the baseline window six months and the follow-up window one month; daily opioid use among the 11 women who used no strip 81.8% to 36.4%; overdose in the past month 6 to 1 women, not significant; at least one harm reduction behaviour after a positive result 33 of 48 (68.8%). Test-strip results and later behaviour (541 adults, 28 days, observational; Gelberg et al., read in full): odds ratio for reporting less rather than the same or more, positive against negative result, 4.37 (3.45 to 5.55) overall, 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27) for illicit benzodiazepines, 10.04 for stimulants only, 4.21 for opioids and stimulants, 2.18 for opioids only, 2.11 for other or unknown drugs; modelled probability of using more after a negative result 0.657 (benzodiazepines), 0.531 (stimulants only), 0.373 (opioids only), 0.225 overall; after a positive result, overall, less or none 0.090, same 0.847, more 0.063. Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents (cited from a preprint); more than 70 people in Dublin. Opioid substitution case notes: retention 72 against 34 and 51 months; in-treatment mortality 1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years (against those prescribed none; lowest in the occasionally prescribed group, no figure given); post-treatment rate in the maintained group 5.90 per 100 years, reported as a 450% rise (4.5 times the in-treatment rate, an increase of about 350%, editors' calculation). Alprazolam rescheduling: 4 of 5 evaluations reported large declines in use; alprazolam-related deaths 57 (2012) to 23 (2015); benzodiazepine overdose deaths 160 (2009) to 238 (2015). Kentucky 'no benzodiazepine' formulary: prescriptions down 89% over two years. Victoria emergency departments, 2020 to 2022: novel benzodiazepine-type drugs in 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%). Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

claims.statement: In people who use drugs in North America who tested their drugs (or, in some studies, their urine) with fentanyl test strips, on their own without supervision or with staff at a supervised injection site (2016 to 2023), a result showing fentanyl was followed, by people's own account or by intentions they stated to staff, by a safer way of using in a minority to a majority of cases, most often using less, going slower or using with someone else around, and seldom by throwing the drug away; in each primary study read, fewer than half said they used, or would use, less; in the largest, most results were followed by using the same amount, and there a result not showing fentanyl was followed more often than one showing it by reports of using more; no study read observed what people then took. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017), of 31 young adults who said a strip had shown fentanyl, 45 in 100 said they then used smaller amounts, 42 went slower, 39 used with someone else around, 36 tried a small amount first (a 'tester'), 10 threw the drugs out, 10 sold them and 7 gave them away; these answers were given at least two weeks later, the results were not checked, and how many used the drugs as usual was not reported. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), staff recorded an intention to use less after 142 of 391 checks before use that showed fentanyl (36 in 100), against 7 of 122 that did not (6 in 100), and an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 (11 in 100) against 10 of 134 (7 in 100); what people then did was not recorded. In a British Columbia take-home programme (2019), asked a standard question (not about their own results) about what they did when a strip showed fentanyl, 217 of 336 answers (65 in 100) described no change, 86 (26 in 100) at least one safer change and 6 (2 in 100) a riskier one (using alone, or using more or faster). In a Baltimore pilot (2018 to 2019), women who sell or trade sex and use opioids were given five strips with training, counselling and naloxone; on average 56 days later, of 48 who answered about a result showing fentanyl, 33 (69 in 100) named at least one safer action, most often using a smaller amount (15, 31 in 100) or going slower when injecting (10, 21 in 100), while 30 (63 in 100) used the tested drugs, several because of withdrawal, 3 threw the drugs out, 3 sold them and none stopped using drugs; of 24 who answered about a result not showing fentanyl, 21 used their drugs as intended (Park et al., 2020). In a cohort of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in Kentucky, New York and Ohio who tested at least once over four weeks in 2023 and reported each week what they had done because of each result (Gelberg et al., 2025), the modelled probabilities after a result showing fentanyl, against one not showing it, were, for the amount used, the same 85 against 75 in 100, less or none 9 against 2 in 100, and more 6 against 23 in 100; and, for other actions, taking turns with someone 24 against 19 in 100, using near someone with naloxone 23 against 15 in 100, a smaller test amount first 12 against 10 in 100, and throwing the drugs away or not using them 1 to 2 in 100 after either result. The cohort's abstract calls the contrast a four-fold reduction in the amount used, but it is an odds ratio for reporting less rather than the same or more, not a measured fall in amount; results and behaviour were self-reported and not checked, and the 541 analysed were those of 1,156 enrolled who completed the surveys, used drugs and tested. A scoping review relays a median of 55 in 100 (23 to 75 in 100, seven studies) reporting some safer change, but its supplementary table shows that the top value counts changes after each result showing fentanyl rather than people and that another is the British Columbia programme's 26 in 100 answers, counted once here; the review also relays people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl; the evidence is mostly intentions or self-reports (one review counts 22 of its 31 behaviour studies as measuring intentions), with no comparison of people given strips with people not given them; both reviews include the Rhode Island and Vancouver studies, and the scoping review the Baltimore pilot, outside its median. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Krieger (31 with a positive result): smaller amounts 45%, went slower 42%, used with someone else 39%, did a tester 36%, threw out 10%, sold 10%, gave away 7%. Karamouzian (checks before use): intended dose reduction 142/391 (36.3%; Wilson 31.7–41.2%) after a positive against 7/122 (5.7%; 2.8–11.4%) after a negative, crude OR 9.36 (4.25–20.65), risk difference 30.6 points (Newcombe 23.3–36.3; editors' calculations); intended disposal 50/436 (11.5%) against 10/134 (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26). Klaire (336 answers to standard questions): no change 217 (64.6%), at least one safer change 86 (25.6%; Wilson 21.2–30.5%), riskier 6 (1.8%; 0.8–3.8%; editors' calculations). Kutscher (relayed): any safer change median 55% (range 23–75%), seven studies, eight locations; Supplemental Table 3: Park et al. (2021) Baltimore 23% and Delaware 69%, Peiper et al. 43%, Oh et al. 56.6%, Klaire et al. 25.6%, Goodman-Meza et al. 53.3%, Arendt 74.9% (changes after each positive detection, among 66 clients), Mema et al. 66.7% (urine testing); median of the eight 54.95% (editors' calculation). Maghsoudi (relayed): 43% of 125 people who inject drugs at a US syringe services programme reported changing behaviour, more often when fentanyl was detected (adjusted OR 5.08, 2.12–12.17). Park 2020 (Baltimore; after a positive result, 48 answering): at least one harm-reduction behaviour 33 (68.8%), used the tested drugs 30 (62.5%), smaller amount 15 (31.3%), went slower 10 (20.8%), tester shot 5 (10.4%), asked someone to check 3 (6.3%), threw out 3, sold 3, told others 6, stopped going to that dealer 2, none stopped using or entered treatment; after a negative result (24 answering), used as intended 21 (87.5%). Gelberg 2025 (three states, 541 people; modelled daily probabilities, positive against negative result): amount less or none 0.090 against 0.023, same 0.847 against 0.752, more 0.063 against 0.225 (odds ratio for reporting less 4.37, 3.45–5.55); took turns 0.24 against 0.19 (ratio 1.29, 1.05–1.59); used near someone with naloxone 0.23 against 0.15 (1.54, 1.16–2.05); used less 0.11 against 0.02 (5.54, 2.52–12.19); used more 0.08 against 0.19 (0.42, 0.26–0.68); used with someone else 0.41 against 0.38; test amount first 0.12 against 0.10; not using 0.02 against 0.02; threw away 0.01 against 0.01; any of 12 changes, using more included, 0.86 against 0.76.
